claim: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a continued threat to human health in both community and healthcare settings.
source: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a continued threat to human health in both community and healthcare settings.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge about MRSA.

claim: MRSA emerges as one of the most widespread and virulent pathogens among antibiotic-resistant agents.
source: Among antibiotic-resistant agents, Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) emerges as one of the most widespread and virulent pathogens (Grundmann et al., 2006; Klevens et al., 2007; Klein et al., 2007; Jarvis et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MRSA has been highlighted as a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
source: has been highlighted as a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) (CDC, 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to CDC report.

claim: MRSA was initially confined to healthcare facilities.
source: Initially confined to healthcare facilities, MRSA has since become increasingly prevalent in the broader population in both the United States and Europe (Chambers, 2001; Naimi et al., 2003; Zetola et al., 2005; Hetem et al., 2012; Kouyos et al., 2013; Tosas Auguet et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MRSA has become increasingly prevalent in the broader population in both the United States and Europe.
source: Initially confined to healthcare facilities, MRSA has since become increasingly prevalent in the broader population in both the United States and Europe (Chambers, 2001; Naimi et al., 2003; Zetola et al., 2005; Hetem et al., 2012; Kouyos et al., 2013; Tosas Auguet et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MRSA can colonize patients without symptoms for years.
source: Further, MRSA can colonize patients without symptoms for years, during which it can be transmitted stealthily (Cooper et al., 2004a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: MRSA can be transmitted stealthily during asymptomatic colonization.
source: Further, MRSA can colonize patients without symptoms for years, during which it can be transmitted stealthily (Cooper et al., 2004a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A general north-south gradient of MRSA prevalence has been observed in Europe, with rare incidence in Scandinavian hospitals and much higher occurrence in Mediterranean hospitals.
source: In Europe, a general north-south gradient has been observed, with rare incidence in Scandinavian hospitals and much higher occurrence in Mediterranean hospitals (Stefani and Varaldo, 2003; Tiemersma et al., 2004; Johnson, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sweden remains one of the few countries with a low prevalence of MRSA infection.
source: In particular, Sweden remains one of the few countries with a low prevalence of MRSA infection (Stenhem et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A substantial proportion of MRSA cases in Sweden has been imported from abroad due to traveling and healthcare contacts in foreign countries.
source: A substantial proportion of MRSA cases in Sweden has been imported from abroad due to traveling and healthcare contacts in foreign countries (Stenhem et al., 2010; Larsson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: No clear clustering of infections in certain wards was observed in the study dataset.
source: In this study dataset, however, we observed no clear clustering of infections in certain wards.
evidence: Based on direct observation of the study data.

claim: Infections are distributed without noticeable clustering, presumably due to effective control measures taken in the study hospitals that maintain a low infection rate even in ICU settings.
source: Infections are distributed without noticeable clustering, presumably due to effective control measures taken in the study hospitals that maintain a low infection rate even in ICU settings (Tiemersma et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on observation of data and inference about the cause, with citation support.

claim: Infected wards tend to have a higher number of inpatients than uninfected wards.
source: Infected wards tend to have a higher number of inpatients, a longer average length of stay as well as a larger ward size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Infected wards tend to have a longer average length of stay than uninfected wards.
source: Infected wards tend to have a higher number of inpatients, a longer average length of stay as well as a larger ward size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Infected wards tend to have a larger ward size than uninfected wards.
source: Infected wards tend to have a higher number of inpatients, a longer average length of stay as well as a larger ward size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The average number of infections is not observed to increase linearly with patient-days.
source: However, the average number of infections is not observed to increase linearly with patient-days, indicating that patient-days per ward alone cannot explain the observed patterns of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patient-days per ward alone cannot explain the observed patterns of infection.
source: However, the average number of infections is not observed to increase linearly with patient-days, indicating that patient-days per ward alone cannot explain the observed patterns of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference based on data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MRSA transmission between colonized/infected patients and susceptible individuals is primarily mediated indirectly by healthcare workers in hospital settings.
source: In hospital settings, MRSA transmission between colonized/infected patients and susceptible individuals is primarily mediated indirectly by healthcare workers (Lowy, 1998; Temime et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The daily in-hospital patient number fluctuates between 4000 and 7000 during the study period.
source: The daily in-hospital patient number fluctuates between 4000 and 7000 during the study period (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Patient hospitalization time, readmission time, and patient-to-patient contact time all follow heavy-tailed distributions, spanning several orders of magnitude.
source: Patient hospitalization time, readmission time, and patient-to-patient contact time all follow heavy-tailed distributions, spanning several orders of magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: About 100 connected components coexist in the contact network each week.
source: Moreover, about 100 connected components coexist in the contact network each week (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: 128,119 patients were transferred from one ward to another during their stay.
source: 128,119 patients were transferred from one ward to another during their stay, and another 280,506 patients were readmitted within 1 year of their previous discharge.
evidence: Based on analysis of hospitalization records.

claim: 280,506 patients were readmitted within 1 year of their previous discharge.
source: 128,119 patients were transferred from one ward to another during their stay, and another 280,506 patients were readmitted within 1 year of their previous discharge.
evidence: Based on analysis of hospitalization records.

claim: All parameter values (β, I₀, C₀) increased in the first 3 or 4 years, and then gradually decreased thereafter.
source: All parameter values increased in the first 3 or 4 years, and then gradually decreased thereafter.
evidence: Based on inference results shown in Figure 3A and Table 2.

claim: The inferred dynamics fit the observed incidence well.
source: The inferred dynamics fit the observed incidence well.
evidence: Based on comparison shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed number of infected wards lies at the peak of the simulated distribution.
source: The observed number lies at the peak of the simulated distribution (vertical dash line).
evidence: Based on comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The observed distribution of infections among wards agrees well with the simulated distributions.
source: In Figure 3D, we compare this distribution obtained from 1000 simulations with what we observed in the data (red diamonds): the observed distribution agrees well with the simulated distributions.
evidence: Based on comparison shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A substantial number of infections are inferred as importations.
source: Figure 3E compares the distributions of both types of infections generated from 1000 simulations: a substantial number of infections are inferred as importations.
evidence: Based on inference results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The number of imported and nosocomial cases obtained from inference generally matches the classification result using days from admission to infection.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, the number of imported and nosocomial cases obtained from inference generally matches the classification result using days from admission to infection.
evidence: Based on comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At its onset, during the first year of the outbreak, UK EMRSA-15 gradually invaded the hospital system from the community with only sporadic nosocomial transmission.
source: Our findings indicate that, at its onset, during the first year of the outbreak, UK EMRSA-15 gradually invaded the hospital system from the community. Only sporadic nosocomial transmission occurred.
evidence: Based on inference of parameters and transmission dynamics.

claim: The simultaneous rise in importation rates may have been caused by household transmission initiated by asymptomatically colonized patients discharged from hospitals.
source: This simultaneous rise may have been caused by household transmission initiated by asymptomatically colonized patients discharged from hospitals.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Both transmission and importation rates were suppressed after the growth phase.
source: After this growth phase, both transmission and importation rates were suppressed.
evidence: Based on inference results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The UK EMRSA-15 outbreak appears near eliminated in Swedish hospitals, represented by the inferred low values of all parameters.
source: Finally, the UK EMRSA-15 outbreak appears near eliminated in Swedish hospitals, represented by the inferred low values of all parameters.
evidence: Based on inference results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: If control measures in hospital were to be relaxed, the colonized patients might spark another outbreak due to the lengthy colonization period.
source: However, if control measures in hospital were to be relaxed, the colonized patients might spark another outbreak due to the lengthy colonization period, which highlights the need for asymptomatic colonization control in order to effect MRSA elimination (Cooper et al., 2004a).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future outcomes, with citation support.

claim: The complex spatiotemporal interaction patterns within the network give rise to a small number of patients with a disproportionately high risk of colonization.
source: The complex spatiotemporal interaction patterns within the network give rise to a small number of patients with a disproportionately high risk of colonization.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed power-law distribution of colonization probability.

claim: High-risk patients tend to appear in densely connected clusters.
source: High-risk patients tend to appear in densely connected clusters.
evidence: Based on visualization shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The proposed intervention strategy can avert considerable numbers of colonization and infection.
source: The findings show that the proposed intervention strategy can avert considerable numbers of colonization and infection (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Decreasing the decolonization threshold leads to a larger screened population and reduces colonization and infection further.
source: Decreasing the decolonization threshold leads to a larger screened population (as shown in the inset of Figure 5B), and thus reduces colonization and infection further.
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The marginal benefit of decreasing the decolonization threshold becomes negligible below a certain threshold value.
source: However, the marginal benefit becomes negligible below a certain threshold value, as the remaining colonized and infected patients are possibly caused by importation, which cannot be directly controlled by inpatient intervention.
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results shown in Figure 5A–B, with inference about the cause.

claim: The decolonization success rate plays an important role in intervention effectiveness.
source: The decolonization success rate also plays an important role, as indicated by the increased colonization and infection for the lower success rate.
evidence: Based on comparison of results with different success rates shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Inference-based screening of approximately 0.89% of all patients can avert up to 38% of infections and 9% of colonizations on average.
source: On average, inference-based screening of approximately 0.89% (6,617/743,599) of all patients can avert up to 38% (121/315) of infections and 9% (1,610/17,810) of colonizations.
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results.

claim: Heuristic control measures based on number of contacts reduced infections and colonizations by 21% and 4%, respectively, given similar numbers of screened patients.
source: In comparison, the other three methods given similar numbers of screened patients only reduced infections and colonizations by 21% and 4% (number of contacts), 27% and 6% (length of stay), and 28% and 6% (contact tracing), respectively.
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: Heuristic control measures based on length of stay reduced infections and colonizations by 27% and 6%, respectively, given similar numbers of screened patients.
source: In comparison, the other three methods given similar numbers of screened patients only reduced infections and colonizations by 21% and 4% (number of contacts), 27% and 6% (length of stay), and 28% and 6% (contact tracing), respectively.
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: Heuristic control measures based on contact tracing reduced infections and colonizations by 28% and 6%, respectively, given similar numbers of screened patients.
source: In comparison, the other three methods given similar numbers of screened patients only reduced infections and colonizations by 21% and 4% (number of contacts), 27% and 6% (length of stay), and 28% and 6% (contact tracing), respectively.
evidence: Based on retrospective control experiment results shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: The inference-based intervention can identify and treat pivotal individuals (superspreaders) who may otherwise transmit MRSA asymptomatically.
source: As a result, the inference-based intervention can identify and treat the pivotal individuals, or superspreaders (Pei and Makse, 2013; Pei et al., 2014; Pei et al., 2017; Pei et al., 2018b; Teng et al., 2016), who may otherwise transmit MRSA asymptomatically in the first place.
evidence: Based on inference from the intervention results, with citations to related work on superspreaders.

claim: The preventive approach of inference-based intervention is more effective than contact tracing in the presence of frequent importation, as it disrupts probable transmission pathways.
source: This preventive approach is more effective than contact tracing in the presence of frequent importation, as it disrupts probable transmission pathways.
evidence: Based on inference from the intervention results.

claim: The dataset contains admission and discharge records of 743,599 distinct patients from 66 hospitals (271 clinics, 1041 wards) in Stockholm County, Sweden.
source: The dataset contains admission and discharge records of 743,599 distinct patients from 66 hospitals (271 clinics, 1041 wards) in Stockholm County, Sweden (Jarynowski and Liljeros, 2015; Rocha et al., 2016), spanning over 3500 continuous days during the 2000s.
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The dataset spans over 3500 continuous days during the 2000s.
source: The dataset contains admission and discharge records of 743,599 distinct patients from 66 hospitals (271 clinics, 1041 wards) in Stockholm County, Sweden (Jarynowski and Liljeros, 2015; Rocha et al., 2016), spanning over 3500 continuous days during the 2000s.
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: A total of 2,041,531 admission records were collected.
source: In total, 2,041,531 admission records were collected.
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The patients constitute over one third of the total 2.2 million population of Stockholm County.
source: The hospitalization dataset is quite comprehensive as the patients constitute over one third of the total 2.2 million population of Stockholm County.
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: A total of 991 positive cases from 172 different strains were confirmed.
source: A total of 991 positive cases from 172 different strains were confirmed, and the most prevalent strain was UK EMRSA-15 (289 cases).
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The most prevalent strain was UK EMRSA-15 (289 cases).
source: A total of 991 positive cases from 172 different strains were confirmed, and the most prevalent strain was UK EMRSA-15 (289 cases).
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: UK EMRSA-15 is present in 16 countries worldwide.
source: UK EMRSA-15 is present in 16 countries worldwide (Grundmann et al., 2010; Das et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Heterogeneity in infection risk exists across different types of ward.
source: Previous studies indicate that heterogeneity in infection risk exists across different types of ward (Bootsma et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Patients in intensive care units (ICUs) typically suffer a higher risk of infection than those in non-ICU settings due to higher patient-healthcare-worker contact rates, high levels of antibiotic use, and high patient vulnerability to infection.
source: For instance, patients in intensive care units (ICUs) typically suffer a higher risk of infection than those in non-ICU settings due to higher patient-healthcare-worker contact rates, high levels of antibiotic use, and high patient vulnerability to infection.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ICU infection risk.

claim: The colonization probability estimated in real time is highly correlated with the results obtained using information from the whole course of the epidemic.
source: The colonization probabilities estimated in real time are highly correlated with the results obtained using information from the whole course of the epidemic, shown in Figure 4C.
evidence: Based on comparison shown in the inset of Figure 5A.
